utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow in the language that I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you, too. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. The purpose of today's sitting is to report on a site visit that the Trial Chamber made or held between the 14th and the 18th of March of this year in Bosnia. The purpose of the visit was to view some of the sites which are relevant to the case. This is the first time ever that such a site visit was held by a Trial Chamber. A few months ago, as you will certainly recall, during one of the sittings, the Trial Chamber sounded the parties on such a possibility. And it was after your positive reaction that we started the ball rolling with a view to establishing first and foremost if it was at all feasible and possible, both from the resources aspect as well as from those aspects which are mainly related to overall security. I need hardly state that holding such an on-site visit is in many significant respects so much different and so much complicated than doing the same thing in a domestic jurisdiction, not to mention the expense involved. From that day until we effectively left for the site visit, the matter was not given any publicity, and discussions here in the courtroom on the matter were held in private session. And this was done for a variety of reasons, particularly, first, because up to a certain stage, we were not quite sure that this would eventually materialise; and secondly, because there were security measures that were being assessed at the time and needed to be established and taken into consideration. I can assure you, however, that in the past months the preparations for the visit entailed a lot of work on the part of several persons here at the Tribunal, but also in Bosnia and elsewhere, as I will explain later on. During the entire visit, the Trial Chamber was accompanied by the two members of -- by two members of its staff, namely, Mr. Ken Roberts, Kenneth Roberts, legal officer; and Mr. Reinhold Gallmetzer, assistant legal officer; as well as by lead counsel for the Prosecution, Madam Joanna Korner; and lead counsel for the Defence, Mr. John Ackerman. Both lead counsel had an interpreter accompanying them. Very early in the discussions held between the Trial Chamber and counsel for the Prosecution and for the accused about the best way to conduct the site visit, it was agreed that the Trial Chamber will, during the site visit, have assisting it as a guide -- have assisting it a guide to be agreed upon by the parties. Mr. Paul Grady was the guide chosen, and he, in fact, accompanied the Trial Chamber during the entire visit. I have mentioned or referred to the discussions that were held between the Trial Chamber and counsel. A substantial part of those discussions centred around the precise set of rules or sort of protocol that everyone taking part on the site visit was or would be expected to abide by. This was imperative, especially since it was not practical that the accused would also take part in the site visit. I need not go into the details of everything that was discussed and decided in the course of these discussions, which included an ad hoc 65 ter meeting, too. It will suffice to state here that there was general agreement that throughout the site visit no submissions will be made by either party and that the visit to each of the locations selected and the relative explanation by the guide, Mr. Grady, would not include any mention or reference to any submission by the Prosecution or to specific facts except insofar as may be agreed upon between the parties. In view of this, the practice was adopted throughout the visit to have both counsel sit with our staff before and in preparation of each daily visit with a view to identifying what the guide would be explaining to the Trial Chamber on the site of each location visited. It may sound cumbersome, or unnecessarily burdensome at first sight to have resorted to such a practice, but I can assure you that it was the best formula under the circumstances; and in addition, that it made it possible for the site visit to be conducted and concluded without any significant hitch. There are several other measures that were put in place, adopted and put in place, relating, for example, to where counsel were lodged in relation to Trial Chamber as well as to the travel arrangements on-site, but I do not think I need go into further details. These arrangements overall were important to have in place and to stick to because we decided to hold this on-site visit in the firm belief that it was best served -- that it would serve best the interests of justice in this case, and also the role of this Tribunal in general. Several locations were visited in this manner on three consecutive days, these being March 15, 16, and 17. The following is a detailed account of the locations visited by the Trial Chamber. Day one, namely, 15th of March: The Trial Chamber visited Omarska camp and where it had the opportunity to go around the camp, various places that it thought fit. We then proceeded to Kevljani village where we stopped to see the mosque. We then proceeded to Kamicani village, which we saw from the road, arriving subsequently in Kozarac where we saw the mosque, Mutnik mosque. And from there, we proceeded to Trnopolje camp which we saw from the road. We then went to Kozarusa village area, which we saw from the road, and proceeded in the direction of Prijedor on the way to Keraterm camp where we stopped for a few minutes. On that occasion, there were also members of the local press present. After that, we proceeded to the city centre in Prijedor. And there we saw the police station, the municipal assembly building, Stari Grad, and what was supposed to be the site of the mosque but not much more. After Prijedor, we proceeded in the direction of Ljubija, and en route, we saw from the road the villages of Hambarine and Brdo. In Ljubija, we stopped to see the football stadium, and from there, we proceeded in the snow to Redak mine area where Mr. Grady indicated to us what he maintained to be an exhumation site. We did not stop to see the site, which incidentally was also partly covered with snow. From there, we proceeded to Carakovo where we saw the Zeger bridge, and from there to Sanski Most where we first of all visited the Krings factory. From the factory, we proceeded to the Sanski Most sports hall, which we stopped to visit. And from there, we proceeded by car through the Mahala area, across the bridge, past Hasan Kikic school, which we viewed from the road. We drove past the municipal building on towards the police station where we stopped and which we visited, particularly the parts of the Sanski Most police station that relate to this case. From there, we proceeded to Betonirka cement factory, and there we visited the three rooms that were indicated to us. From the Betonirka factory, we proceeded to the Partisan cemetery, which we viewed from the road, and drove on to Vrhpolje bridge where we stopped for a few minutes. We were also shown at Vrhpolje bridge on one of the banks of the river another exhumation site that Mr. Grady identified and indicated to us. Past Vrhpolje bridge, we proceeded to Hrustovo village. We had an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occasion to view Begici bridge, and particularly the Kukavice -- a house in Kukavice, which is related to the present case. We left Hrustovo to proceed to Kerani. In Kerani we only viewed the old mosque. And from there, we proceeded back to our hotel. And that concludes the first day. The second day, that is, the 16th of March, started with a visit to Manjaca camp. In Manjaca camp, we had an opportunity to enter into the administration building, the building which we were informed was the infirmary, and we visited also several of the so-called stables, both in the front and in the back row. From Manjaca, we proceeded to the SFOR base, Maple Leaf Base, in Velecevo -- at ZGON, and there we had a helicopter flight to and over Vlasic mountain in the Korcani area. En route, we were shown several other locations, particularly Prhovo and Pec. Back on land, we proceeded to Kljuc, the village of Kljuc. And in Kljuc, we saw the police station, Nikola Mackic school. And from there, we proceeded to Pudin Han, which we saw from the road, on our way to Velegici school area. There, we saw the Velegici school as well as the monument -- the Velegici school area, because the school does not exist any more, and the monument that there is now. And from there, we departed to the direction of Biljani. In Biljani, we saw the mosque. From Biljani, we were assured that the roads were no longer covered with snow, and we proceeded to Laniste, finding that the roads were pretty well covered with snow. And in Laniste Mr. Grady pointed to us another exhumation site. From Laniste, we went back to our hotel, passing through Sanski Most once more. On day three of the visit, namely, the 17th of March, we visited first Celinac, which we -- in which we saw the municipal building from outside and also the hotel that is across the park where the SDS had its first meeting. We arrived from there in Kotor Varos, where we visited the sawmill. Then on foot, we walked to the direction of the Croat or Catholic church, in the vicinity of the sawmill. And we then drove past the municipality building. We did not see the courthouse, as we had planned to, because we missed it, and it was not practical to turn back to see the courthouse, inside of which we had not meant to go in any case. But in Kotor Varos, we also saw the elementary school, and we visited the police station, particularly the detention cells in the police station. We also saw the medical centre. We did not go inside the medical centre. And from the medical centre, we proceeded to Stari Zatvor. We saw Stari Zatvor gaol from the road, and from there, we proceeded in the direction of Kotor Varos, seeing the Cirkin Brdo area. We saw the Hanifici mosque. And from there, from Hanifici village, we proceeded to Vecici. In Vecici, we spent some time. We saw the mosque, and also a monument that has been erected in the vicinity of the mosque. From Vecici, we proceeded to Dabovici. In the Dabovici area, we saw Kukavice and the surroundings areas. We proceeded to Grabovice school, which is still there, but we were informed that the inside layout had been changed, and we therefore decided not to go inside. And from there, we proceeded to Banja Luka. In Banja Luka, we saw the CSB building and the municipal building from outside. We also had a view of the old 1st Krajina Corps headquarters from the road. We did stop for a while at the Mali Logor prison where we also had an occasion to meet with a senior member of the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska -- of Republika Srpska, who extended his welcome as well as his full cooperation. That is, in brief, an account of the places which we visited in the course of our site visit. Now, the whole exercise, and I am sure I have the consensus of everyone present here, the whole exercise, the whole site visit would not have been possible and would not have been a success had it not been for the cooperation of several persons, as well as institutions. And we therefore wish to express our thanks and gratitude to each and every one of these persons. I will not mention every single person that participated in this whole venture and to whom we shall in due course by means of letters express our thanks but here, publicly, I wish to thank several persons in particular. And I will start with you, Ms. Korner, and of course your team; and you, Mr. Ackerman, and of course your team, because had you not cooperated fully as you did, there's no way we could have held such a site visit, and there is no way that the site visit itself would have gone on as smoothly as we all know it did. So my first thanks go to you. I then need to thank from the bottom of my heart, and that's not just my heart, but also Judge Janu and Judge Taya, our President, who encouraged this site visit and who extended his help; the Registrar of this Tribunal, Mr. Holthuis, and his deputy, Mr. Tolbert, with whom we had discussions as we went along. Of course, the chief budget officer that had to dig into the finances or the funds of this Tribunal to make this happen. That's on the side of the -- the management side or administration side of this Tribunal. On the side also -- on the part of this Tribunal also, there's no way we could have proceeded with this on-site visit had it not been for the full cooperation of the security branch. And therefore, I wish to thank Mr. Nick Innell, the chief of security's operation, and Mr. Peter Zmiyarch, the security operations officer; and last, but certainly not least in this area, the four officers that accompanied us during the visit; namely, Lieutenant Maurice Ford, Officer Dantand, and Sergeants Lyne and Peoples. I wish, of course, to thank Mr. Paul Grady who guided us through the various sites according to the agreement that was reached between the parties from day to day. Mr. Grady, I think, did a wonderful job. And of course, I wish to thank the field officers. There was more than one field officer involved, because we were both in Croatia, in Republika Srpska, and in the Federation. So I wish to thank Mr. Barry Hogan from the Banja Luka field office; Mr. Jani Aaltonen, security officer, member of the advance team, also from the Banja Luka field office; and Mr. Thomas Osorio and his deputy from the Zagreb field office. Not only for their hospitality, but also for their assistance. During our stay there, also we had the assistance of SFOR, several people -- several persons involved. I will just mention two of them. One is Brigadier General Stuart Beare, and the other one is Major Brandon Kew. The first is responsible for the multinational brigade north-west section, and he left no stone unturned in his efforts to ensure that everything went according to plan. Major Kew was responsible for the helicopter flight, and he also hosted us to lunch, the entire group, after we landed back from our trip to -- over Vlasic mountain. So I thank the brigadier general and major for their assistance. And I will finish with perhaps the persons who extended not only their cooperation, their full cooperation, but who also made it possible for us to be able to go on this site visit. We visited Croatia on our way to Republika Srpska and the federation. We visited Republika Srpska, various places in Republika Srpska. We visited also places in the federation. This involved the cooperation of the authorities in these areas. It was a pleasure on the first night when we arrived there to see Mr. Trivun Jovicic, who I also recognise in the gallery today, visiting us, welcoming us as the Serb minister councillor for Serb nationality and the Serb liaison officer for Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I wish to thank you, sir, for all the cooperation that we had in the course of our visit to the various areas in Republika Srpska. I also want to thank Mr. Amir Ahmic, who is also Minister Counselor for Bosniak nationality and who is your counterpart, that is, the Bosniak liaison officer for Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I say liaison officer, liaison officer with the ICTY. I thank you both. I also wish to thank Mr. Goran Mihaljevic, Minister Counselor for Croat nationality and who happens also to be the Croat liaison officer for Bosnia and Herzegovina with this Tribunal. The three of you cooperated together, and it was a pleasure for all of us to see the extent of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cooperation that exists in the country between you and your officers. I wish at the same time to express our thanks and gratitude for your governments, the respective governments of the federation and also of Republika Srpska. And I also wish to extend our thanks to the chief of administration for the respective police forces who provided us with escort throughout our visit in a most efficient manner. I wish to thank your governments. I also wish to thank the government of Croatia, Mr. Frene Krnic, Ambassador of Croatia in The Hague, for all the cooperation that you extended for the purpose of and in the course of our site visit. On the penultimate day, I had -- we had an occasion to meet with Mr. Milorad Jelisavac personally. He came to see us, to visit us. We had practically finished our visit. We only needed -- we had left Banja Luka. It was very nice of him and very courteous of him to join us and we also express to him our gratitude, but I do want to mention his name here as well because most of the time we were in Republika Srpska, and it was no easy job for the police escort that was provided by Republika Srpska just as it wasn't easy for the rest. I thank you all. I finish by stating that we think we did the right thing. We believe we did the right thing in having this on-site visit. We learned a lot. And it will be -- put us in a better position to understand some of the events that we have heard evidence about. And it will put us in a better position when we come to elaborate our final judgement and reach several decisions that we need to take. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention before Your Honour rises one aspect which is unconnected with this visit that has recently come to my notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The judgement of...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I knew exactly. I was going to mention it myself if none of you mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has come down finally. And therefore, we will address the matter in our final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I expect you to, obviously. I expect you to. And that applies to you as well, Mr. Ackerman. It does change a little bit the scenario. I think more or less what we need you to express is how the change that is the result of the decision of the Appeals Chamber will impact this case. I don't know to what extent, but please, we expect you to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I was going to say, Your Honour. We propose to address it in our legal submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And if we think that -- we still have to discuss it at some length amongst ourselves, but if we think there is place for some further communication to you specifically addressing this point, we will come back to you, as we did on other issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second matter is this: In the Court Calendar for the 15th of April it is said that the judgement in Krstic will be given. Your Honour, that may -- first of all, if it's confirmed -- I know it's there, but that doesn't necessarily mean that it will be handed down on that day -- it could possibly have an impact on the submissions that will be made on genocide and indeed other matters. We are due to file the response of the Prosecution to the Defence final brief, and vice versa, on the 16th. If the judgement is handed down then, that would only give us less than a day. We would ask for an extension until the Monday, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it in a different manner, Ms. Korner. We are aware almost hundred per cent of the areas which Krstic could touch upon, Appeals Chamber could touch upon in Krstic and which could impact our labours. What I'm going to suggest is that these do not constitute the majority of issues that we need to address. So please go ahead with the final briefs as planned, and then depending on how the Krstic appeals judgement might impact, you will have an extension or the possibility to file an addendum to your final brief. But it's important that on the 16th April you put us at least in a position where we need to know exactly what your position is on the other matters. I suppose also on the matters that will be covered in Krstic, with the caveat that if the situation changes because of the decision in Krstic, then obviously you will have an opportunity to present again your views on those particular matters. At least you would put us in a position where, starting from the 16th, we would be able to fill in what we need to fill in in the various bits and pieces we will be drafting by then. I suppose that you should be able to live with that. I don't think it should create any major problems for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The purpose of the response is to deal with any legal submissions that the Defence make which we say are perhaps incorrect, and vice versa, and also any factual matters that we disagree with. The only thing that concerns me slightly, and it's jumping the gun slightly because we have no idea what the decision is going to be, is that we're supposed to be making -- I'm supposed to start my final address on the Tuesday. And if there's a dramatic change, then it may be a little difficult. Your Honour, can I put it this way, that Your Honour is aware of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be moving to Monday, not even Tuesday. When I told you that I need the 23rd clear, of that month. Let's play it by ear, Ms. Korner, and Mr. Ackerman. First of all, I haven't heard you, Mr. Ackerman, but my instinct would tell me to play it by the ear. First we see what the Appeals Chamber will say in that other case, then we might ourselves come back and suggest to you that we also need time to consider the position as it relates to certain issues. So it hasn't -- I don't think you need to worry about it, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All I'm doing at this moment, Your Honour, is putting Your Honour in the picture, as I'm sure Your Honours would have been, to say that we may need, however it's worked out, further time to deal with the matters of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you this is all on our mind constantly. And this morning, I was even checking on how possible it is to expect the appeals decision also in another case that can affect our case, particularly in the areas of deportation, for example, forcible transfer. But not only. Well, I will have confirmation of what the situation is likely to be on that other case in about two weeks' time, but not now. Krstic definitely we are expecting it when you say. If it creates problems, you will have the time you require to put you in a -- it doesn't make sense for us to impose a closure on you when we need to hear what you have to say in any case, and we also need to study the matters as they may emerge after the Krstic appeals decision. So we will play it by the ear. If we need to give you an extension for additional written submissions, we will. It may well be that you would prefer not to resort to written submissions but to include your fresh submissions in your oral presentations, closings. I don't know. We will be open for any suggestions that you might have and we will definitely not foreclose on you and deprive you from filing additional submissions. Definitely not. If you need more time, we will give you more time. But do make sure that at least the basic final briefs will be filed when we have agreed that they will be filed, because we need those. We are already working, obviously, on the judgement, but working relatively speaking, because we can only work up to here, not knowing what your final submissions are going to be. So we will definitely not present you with any difficulties. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things very briefly. In your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remarks, you were speaking of our visit to Celinac and you mentioned that we saw the hotel where the first SDS meeting occurred. It wasn't the first SDS meeting, it was the organisational meeting of the ZOBK, I think, is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to correct that for the record before it confused anyone. The other thing, I just want to join you in thanking everyone that you thanked, and I think I should particularly single out Mr. Paul Grady who I believe behaved in the highest degree of professionalism with regard to his behaviour on this trip, and I think that contributed a great deal to making it a success. And I must tell you that I had some trepidations about that as we began, but they were totally unjustified. I think he deserves to hear that from me. And other than that, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. The three of us share your sense of appreciation for the work done by Mr. Grady. It was indeed very professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Grady, who is not in Court, we are very grateful to Your Honours and to Mr. Ackerman. It was, for Mr. Grady, a really difficult task, not only having to plot all the areas in advance, but because this was a combined Defence/Prosecution effort, he had to be really careful about what he said. And as Your Honours know, he took exceptional trouble to make sure that he dealt with things correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That is very true, Ms. Korner. And I don't think we need to add more to that. We also ensured as much as we could - of course it doesn't always happen like that - in the course of the visit we tried to stick together all of us most of the time because that was always -- that was very important. Of course, there were exceptions when I myself would drift aside or... But I'm pretty sure that everything was very much transparent and that, to my knowledge at least, there are no reservations on the way the whole site visit was conducted. Having said that, I bring this sitting to an end. And we will await the Appeals Chamber decision in the other case, possibly in both. The understanding is in the Stakic case it will be too late in the day if we get a decision before our final decision to reopen discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Stakic appeal hasn't even been heard, Your Honour. It's way off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but there's a Status Conference in two weeks' time. And depending on that, a decision will be taken whether it will be handed down before the summer recess or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that will come as a surprise to everybody in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Me, too. But it's only fair that I put you into the picture. As things stand, it's not likely that we will have a direction from the Appeals Chamber on those issues before we hand down our decision. Thank you. And good afternoon.
